title: Pray for one another (James 5:13–20)
hookLine: sick? call the elders; suffering? pray; cheerful? sing

cards: Some letters end with a long goodbye. James doesn't. No greetings, no names, no farewell.
His last paragraph reads like a list on the fridge before a long trip: if this happens, do this. Sad? Happy?
Sick? Wandering? There's an instruction for each.
And almost every one points to the same thing. Not a technique, not a rule. Other people, and prayer.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms." Every mood has a place to go: hard days, bring them to God; good days, sing.
Then: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves.
The sick person calls, and the elders come to the bedside. Oil was a common medicine in the ancient world, and also a sign of being set apart for God. Churches practice this verse differently.

For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, it's one of the roots of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestant churches also anoint and pray over the sick, as a practice of prayer rather than a sacrament.

teach.h: CONFESS AND PRAY, ONE TO ANOTHER.
teach.b: Then: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." One to another: not only up to God, but sideways, to each other.
Elijah, he says, was a man subject to like passions as we are. An ordinary human, moody, tired, frightened at times.
He prayed, and rain was held back; he prayed again, and it came. You don't need to be a giant; ordinary people's prayers matter.

The very last line: whoever brings back someone who has wandered from the truth saves a soul and covers a multitude of sins. The letter ends not with a farewell, but with someone going after someone else.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament based in part on James 5:14–15, and many Protestant churches have elders or ministers anoint and pray over the sick; most churches also pray for the sick by name in worship.

games.q: someone in your church is seriously ill. according to James, what happens?
o: they wait quietly for it to pass.
they call the elders, who pray over them and anoint them with oil.
games.why: "let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."

practice: Think of someone who is ill right now, a friend, a parent, a child, someone you've only heard about, and picture where they are and what they might be feeling.
If you pray, pray for them by name in your own words, one for another, as James says; if you don't, hold them in your attention with care and wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Elders. The ones the sick are told to call in James's last instructions: come to the bedside, pray, anoint with oil, and hold each other up.

orig.note: Greek: elder. the root of the English words priest and Presbyterian.

carryVoice: Your line: going after someone who wandered. That's where James chooses to end his letter. Six hundred eighty days, and counting.
